newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH - Budget bills update - overview.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH - Budget bills update - overview.

text.p: Thursday has seen only small progress on budget bills, but there has been a reassuring sign for the government that the outstanding fiscal measures may get Independent support.
The Senate is currently dealing with Higher Education Legislation Amendment Bill, which is worth a total of A$296 million to the budget in 1997/98.
The government, it must be remembered at all times in watching budget bills, needs two more votes from somewhere -- anywhere -- to get a measure through the Senate.
There are four sources of those two votes: Labor, the Australian Democrats, the two Greens, or the two Independents, if they vote together.
So the crisis point for the government comes if Labor, the Democrats and the Greens all withhold support.

The Higher Education Bill would do two things. It would raise student charges on some courses (A$66 million in 1997/98) and it would trigger faster repayments of student debts (A$230 million in 1997/98).

The important thing that happened today is that Brian Harradine, one of the Independents, said: "If it's a choice between HECS (Higher Education Contribution Scheme) increases and severe reductions to recurrent grants for universities then obviously the former is the less undesirable."
If the other Independent, Mal Colston, thinks the same way then this bill will go through.
One wonders whether Harradine could be similarly persuaded on the entire budget by Treasurer Peter Costello's Wednesday threat to raise taxes if the Senate mangled the fiscal measures.
That is, Harradine may regret the cuts but sees them as preferable to a tax hike.
Costello late on Wednesday issued new estimates of how much the budget lost in the Tuesday amendments to the bill that would have excluded immigrants from social security for two years.
Effectively, Costello has confirmed the A$400 million-over-four-years estimate given by Social Security Minister Jocelyn Newman.
This seems to correct Costello's earlier estimate of A$200 million-over-four-years.
Expressing the budget loss in more meaningful single-year figures, Newman's office has estimated that the changes will cost A$130 million in 1997/98.

In addition, some higher court fees were interfered with by the Senate. Canberra Watch has not identified the cost of the changes, but it must be less than A$27 million that the government hoped to raise in 1997/98.
